Anatomical white matter tracts span the cortical hierarchy to support cognitive diversity

The cerebral cortex is organized into distinct functional areas or "subdivisions" that emerge during development under graded morphogen and transcription factor (TF) patterns 2. These early molecular gradients (e.g. anterior FGF vs posterior Wnt/BMP sources) set up opposing gradients of TFs (such as Pax6 anteriorly and Emx2 posteriorly) that impart positional identity to cortical progenitors (cells that are pre-differentiation). As a result, the adult cortex contains four canonical "primary" areas - visual (V1), auditory (A1), somatosensory (S1) and motor (M1) - each tied to a specific modality and its corresponding thalamic relays. In broad strokes, the occipital cortex is specialized for vision, the superior temporal lobe for audition and language-related processing, the postcentral gyrus and adjacent parietal lobe for somatosensation and spatial processing, and the frontal lobe (including premotor and prefrontal regions) for motor control, executive function and higher cognition. These lobar and areal subdivisions are reflected in cytoarchitectonic differences and in the patterns of long-range connections that interlink them.

The flow of information into and out of the cortex follows "highway" pathways in the white matter. All sensory modalities project via the thalamus into specific cortical areas: for example, the optic radiations carry visual signals from the lateral geniculate nucleus to V1, the acoustic radiations from the medial geniculate nucleus to A1, and dorsal column/medial lemniscus projections from the ventral posterolateral thalamus to S1. In fact, the thalamus is the major hub sending axons to the entire cortical mantle, establishing modality-specific projection tracts early in development 3. Motor output pathways (e.g. corticospinal fibers via the internal capsule and corona radiata) likewise leave frontal motor cortex and descend to subcortical and spinal targets. These projection fibers - sometimes called the corona radiata, internal capsule, and specific radiations - define the feedforward sensory streams and feedback motor streams. Commissural fibers in the corpus callosum provide the main interhemispheric highway, linking homologous regions of the two hemispheres and enabling bilateral integration of sensory and motor maps. Together, thalamocortical, corticofugal, and commissural tracts form the core "subcortical highways" for sending raw sensory data into the cortex and distributing cortical output, while respecting the functional layout of cortical subdivisions.

Within each hemisphere, long-range association tracts interconnect cortical areas according to functional streams. Prominent dorsal-stream tracts (often termed the superior longitudinal system) run anteroposteriorly: for example, the superior longitudinal fasciculus (SLF) and its arcuate fasciculus branch link frontal regions with parietal and occipital cortices 4. These dorsal pathways underlie spatial "where" processing and coordinate fronto-parietal attention and sensorimotor integration. In contrast, the ventral-stream or inferior longitudinal system carries information between occipital/temporal and frontal lobes. The inferior fronto‑occipital fasciculus (IFOF) and uncinate fasciculus (UF) run beneath the insula, connecting anterior temporal and occipital regions to frontal cortex. Likewise, the inferior longitudinal fasciculus (ILF) courses ventrally to join occipital visual areas with anterior temporal cortex, supporting object and face recognition ("what" pathway). Medial association tracts include the cingulum bundle, which arches within the cingulate gyrus to interconnect medial frontal, parietal and hippocampal regions, supporting the limbic and default-mode networks. (In parallel, short U-fibers link neighboring gyri, and multiple parallel sub-branches of these major systems fan out to diverse targets.) In sum, each cortical subdivision tends to exchange information with appropriate partners via these large fasciculi: for instance, visual cortices connect to parietal (dorsal) and temporal (ventral) cortices via SLF/AF, ILF and IFOF; auditory and language areas in superior temporal lobe connect to inferior frontal (Broca’s) regions via the arcuate; somatosensory areas connect to motor regions via local U-fibers and the SLF; and prefrontal areas receive convergent inputs from many of these streams. The overall architecture ensures that unimodal sensory regions feed into higher association cortices, while distributed frontal and parietal regions can rapidly communicate through the dorsal "belt" and the ventral "ventral belt" of fibers. These pathways are not random but emerge from developmental patterning. The genetic protomap of the cortex sets up a scaffold of areal identity 2, and axon guidance molecules (ephrin gradients, netrins, semaphorins, etc.) steer fibers into the correct white‐matter highways. For example, retinotopic maps form in concert with graded Eph/ephrin signaling in both retina-to-LGN and LGN-to-V1 projections. Similarly, corticothalamic and thalamocortical fibers navigate through the internal capsule under the influence of "handshake" interactions and gradient cues 3. In effect, early molecular gradients and midline patterning centers anchor the broad topology of cortical subdivisions, and subsequent chemoaffinity and activity-dependent processes refine the specific tracts between them. The result is a genetically-guided organization in which chemical gradients foreshadow the adult functional layout: e.g. anterior‐posterior gene gradients align with frontal-vs-occipital specializations, which in turn align with the course of major association fascicles. Over time, ongoing activity and plasticity further sculpt these highways (e.g. via pruning or myelination) so that the structural connectivity faithfully maps the information flow demands of vision, audition, sensation, and higher cognition across the cortical sheet.
